lead.en: A shot in Sarajevo brings down four empires

summary.en: The assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand in Sarajevo in June 1914 drew the great powers into a war of the Entente against Germany and its allies. It killed millions and brought down the German, Austro-Hungarian, Russian and Ottoman empires.

lead.en: Ships no longer have to round Cape Horn

summary.en: Ferdinand de Lesseps's French attempt in the 1880s failed after malaria and yellow fever killed, by various estimates, more than 20,000 people. The US started again in 1904, beat the mosquitoes and built a system of locks with the artificial Gatún Lake. The 82-km canal opened on 15 August 1914, cutting the New York to San Francisco voyage by almost 13,000 km. It was handed to Panama in 1999.

title.en: Death of Martha, the last passenger pigeon

lead.en: The bird whose flocks once darkened the sky is gone forever

summary.en: On 1 September 1914 Martha, the last passenger pigeon, died at the Cincinnati Zoo. In the 19th century it was perhaps North America's most numerous bird, with flocks of billions darkening the sky. The world barely noticed: World War I had begun a month earlier.

lead.en: Enemies leave the trenches to sing carols and play football

summary.en: At Christmas 1914, five months into the war, British, French and German soldiers on many sectors of the front stopped shooting without orders. They met in no man's land, swapped food and souvenirs, sang carols together and, by many accounts, played football.

lead.en: Deportations and massacres destroyed Anatolia's Armenians

place.en: Anatolia to the Syrian desert (Deir ez-Zor)

summary.en: On 24 April 1915 hundreds of Armenian community leaders were arrested in Constantinople. The Young Turk government then began mass deportations of Armenians to the Syrian desert; columns perished from killings, hunger and disease. By various estimates 600,000 to 1.5 million died. Many states and most historians recognise it as genocide; Turkey rejects that characterisation.

lead.en: A failed push on Istanbul becomes a day of ANZAC remembrance

summary.en: Allied troops, including Australians and New Zealanders (ANZAC), landed on the Gallipoli peninsula to force a way to Istanbul but withdrew after eight months. The defeat made Mustafa Kemal famous, and 25 April became a day of remembrance in Australia and New Zealand.

lead.en: 9-metre wheels — and it got stuck on its very first test

summary.en: Engineer Lebedenko won over Nicholas II with a wind-up model powered by a gramophone spring. The real machine had front wheels almost 9 m across, but in tests in August 1915 its small rear roller sank in soft ground. It rusted in the forest for six more years before being scrapped.

lead.en: The secret deal behind the map of the modern Middle East

place.en: Arab provinces of the Ottoman Empire

summary.en: In May 1916 British diplomat Mark Sykes and Frenchman François Georges-Picot secretly divided the Ottoman Arab lands into spheres: Syria and Lebanon for France, Mesopotamia for Britain, Palestine under international administration. The Bolsheviks published the text in 1917. The League of Nations mandates largely followed these lines.

lead.en: The Sharif of Mecca rises against the sultan, with Lawrence

summary.en: In June 1916 Sharif Hussein bin Ali of Mecca, promised Arab independence by Britain, rose against the Ottomans. His son Faisal and British officer T. E. Lawrence raided the Hejaz Railway, took Aqaba in 1917 and entered Damascus in October 1918. The promised unified Arab state never materialised.

lead.en: The Bolsheviks seize power and found a socialist state

summary.en: On 25 October (7 November) 1917 the Bolsheviks led by Lenin overthrew the Provisional Government and seized the Winter Palace. The world's first socialist state was born, and the seizure of power was followed by the Russian Civil War.

lead.en: Reds against Whites — millions dead and mass emigration

summary.en: After the October Revolution the Bolsheviks fought White armies, national movements and foreign interventions. The war claimed an estimated 7–12 million lives, drove mass emigration and ended in victory for the Red Army.

lead.en: Nicholas II abdicates and Russia's monarchy falls

summary.en: Strikes and bread riots in Petrograd in February 1917 grew into an uprising joined by the garrison. Nicholas II abdicated, the monarchy fell, and power passed to the Provisional Government, which shared it uneasily with the Petrograd Soviet.

lead.en: A British pledge at the root of the Palestine question

summary.en: On 2 November 1917 British Foreign Secretary Arthur Balfour wrote to Lord Rothschild pledging support for 'a national home for the Jewish people' in Palestine, provided nothing prejudiced the civil and religious rights of its non-Jewish communities, then about 90% of the population. The pledge was written into the League of Nations Mandate for Palestine; the parties to the conflict still view it in sharply different ways.

lead.en: Two girls photograph fairies, and Conan Doyle believes them

summary.en: In 1917 cousins Elsie, 16, and Frances, 9, took photos of themselves with 'fairies' by a stream. Sherlock Holmes's creator Arthur Conan Doyle hailed them as proof that fairies exist. Only in the early 1980s did the cousins admit the fairies were cardboard cut-outs copied from a children's book.

lead.en: Flu infects a third of humanity and kills more than the war

summary.en: One of the first recorded outbreaks hit a Kansas army camp in March 1918, though the virus's origin is still debated. Troops spread it worldwide, infecting about a third of humanity. Estimates of deaths range from 17 to 50 million, more than the war itself killed.

title.en: Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes

lead.en: The South Slavs unite in what will become Yugoslavia

summary.en: On 1 December 1918, after Austria-Hungary collapsed, a united South Slav kingdom was proclaimed under Serbia's Karađorđević dynasty. From 1929 it was called Yugoslavia.

title.en: Death of the last Carolina parakeet

lead.en: The eastern US loses its only native parrot

summary.en: On 21 February 1918 Incas, the last known Carolina parakeet, the only parrot native to the eastern United States, died at the same Cincinnati Zoo as Martha. Wild sightings were reported later, but the species was declared extinct in 1939.

title.en: Cher Ami saves the Lost Battalion

lead.en: A wounded pigeon stops friendly artillery fire

summary.en: In October 1918 a surrounded American battalion came under fire from its own guns. The pigeon Cher Ami, shot through the breast and losing a leg, reached headquarters with a note; the shelling stopped and 194 men survived.

lead.en: Peace terms that help sow the Second World War

summary.en: Signed in the Hall of Mirrors at Versailles, the treaty formally ended the First World War with Germany. Germany lost its colonies and some territory, had its army limited and was made to pay reparations, a humiliation that helped bring on the Second World War.

lead.en: A wave of molasses sweeps the streets at 35 mph

summary.en: On 15 January 1919 a tank holding 8,700 cubic metres of molasses burst in Boston. A sticky wave swept through the North End at about 35 mph, killing 21 people. For decades afterwards residents insisted the neighbourhood still smelled of molasses on hot days.

lead.en: The first worldwide organisation to keep the peace

summary.en: On 10 January 1920 the Covenant of the League of Nations, created after the First World War with its headquarters in Geneva, came into force. The League was meant to settle disputes peacefully, but the United States never joined and it failed to stop Japanese, Italian and German aggression in the 1930s. The United Nations replaced it in 1946.

lead.en: Music from thin air: played without being touched

summary.en: In October 1920 the physicist Lev Termen demonstrated an instrument whose pitch changes as the player's hands move near two antennas. In 1922 he was invited to the Kremlin, where Lenin himself tried to play Glinka's 'The Lark' on it. Termen later toured Europe and the USA with it.

lead.en: Four republics sign a treaty forming a new union

summary.en: On 30 December 1922 the Russian SFSR, Ukrainian SSR, Byelorussian SSR and Transcaucasian SFSR signed the treaty creating the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics. The USSR became the world's largest state by area and a leading force of the 20th century.

title.en: March on Rome: Mussolini takes power

lead.en: Europe's first fascist regime takes power

summary.en: In October 1922 Blackshirt squads marched on Rome, and King Victor Emmanuel III asked Benito Mussolini to form a government. Within a few years he turned Italy into a one-party dictatorship.

lead.en: A nearly intact pharaoh's tomb in the Valley of the Kings

summary.en: On 4 November 1922 Howard Carter's workmen cleared a step leading to a sealed tomb in the Valley of the Kings. Three weeks later Carter peered in by candlelight and, asked by Lord Carnarvon whether he could see anything, replied: 'Yes, wonderful things.' The tomb held more than 5,000 objects, including a gold mask of about 10 kg. The find set off worldwide Egyptomania.

lead.en: Brazil seeks its own voice — its modernism begins

summary.en: In February 1922, marking a century of Brazilian independence, modernist painters, poets and musicians staged a festival at São Paulo's Municipal Theatre. It launched Brazilian modernism and the search for a distinctly national culture.

lead.en: Tremors and fire whirls destroy Tokyo and Yokohama

summary.en: On 1 September 1923, at lunchtime when many cooking fires were lit, an earthquake struck Tokyo and Yokohama. Fires and firestorms completed the destruction, killing over 100,000 people. In the chaos, mobs massacred Korean residents.

lead.en: Turkey secures the borders it still holds today

summary.en: On 24 July 1923 Turkey signed a peace at Lausanne with the Allied powers and Greece, replacing the punitive Treaty of Sèvres. Victory in the War of Independence let the Kemalists win recognition of almost all of Turkey's present borders and the abolition of the capitulations. A separate convention confirmed a population exchange: about 1.2 million Orthodox Christians left Turkey and some 400,000 Muslims left Greece.

title.en: Proclamation of the Republic of Turkey

lead.en: Atatürk builds a secular state from an empire's remains

summary.en: On 29 October 1923, after the War of Independence and the abolition of the sultanate, the Republic of Turkey was proclaimed in Ankara. Its first president, Mustafa Kemal Atatürk, pushed through secular reforms that turned the Ottoman heartland into a modern nation-state.

lead.en: Bold editing and the Odessa Steps reshape film language

summary.en: In December 1925 Sergei Eisenstein's film about the 1905 naval mutiny premiered at the Bolshoi Theatre. Its pioneering montage, above all the Odessa Steps sequence, made it one of the most influential films ever made.

lead.en: A dog meets his master's train for nearly ten years

summary.en: The Akita Hachikō met Professor Ueno at Shibuya Station every day. Ueno died at work in May 1925, but the dog kept coming to meet the train almost daily until his own death in March 1935. His bronze statue was unveiled in 1934 while he was still alive, and Hachikō attended the ceremony.

lead.en: Baird transmits moving human faces for the first time

summary.en: On 26 January 1926 Scottish inventor John Logie Baird showed scientists in London's Soho a transmission of moving images of human faces. Mechanical television soon gave way to electronic systems developed by Vladimir Zworykin, Philo Farnsworth and others.

lead.en: A prankster lawyer leaves his fortune to the most prolific mother

summary.en: Toronto lawyer and practical joker Charles Millar died in 1926, leaving his estate to the Toronto woman who bore the most children in the next ten years. The race ran until 1936; a judge split the prize among four mothers with nine children each, who got $110,000 apiece.

title.en: The Jazz Singer and the talkies

lead.en: The screen starts talking and silent film fades

summary.en: In October 1927 Warner Bros. released The Jazz Singer starring Al Jolson, the first feature-length film with synchronised songs and dialogue. Its success ended the silent film era within a few years.

lead.en: The longest lab experiment: one drop a decade

summary.en: In 1927 Professor Thomas Parnell put pitch, a tar that looks solid and shatters under a hammer, into a funnel to show students it is really a liquid. Only nine drops have fallen since, and nobody has ever seen one actually fall.

lead.en: A mould kills bacteria — the first mass antibiotic

summary.en: In September 1928 Alexander Fleming noticed that a mould in a Petri dish was killing bacteria. Penicillin, purified from it in the 1940s by Florey and Chain, became the first mass-produced antibiotic and saved millions of lives.

lead.en: Magnitka and Dneproges: the USSR builds industry at speed

summary.en: In 1928–1932 the USSR pursued forced industrialisation under its first five-year plan. The Magnitogorsk steelworks, the Dnieper hydroelectric station, the Stalingrad tractor plant and hundreds of other plants were built.

title.en: Wall Street Crash and the Great Depression

lead.en: A stock crash triggers the century's worst slump

summary.en: In October 1929 share prices collapsed on the New York Stock Exchange. The crash ushered in the Great Depression, the worst economic crisis of the 20th century, bringing mass unemployment worldwide and feeding the rise of radical movements.

lead.en: Peasants are forced into collective farms, "kulaks" deported

summary.en: From 1929 Soviet peasant farms were forcibly merged into collective farms. Those who resisted were branded 'kulaks', and some two million people were deported to special settlements. Collectivisation caused a sharp fall in agricultural output.

title.en: The Soviet five-day week abolishes Sunday

lead.en: Each worker's day off had a colour — spouses' often differed

summary.en: From autumn 1929 Soviet factories ran nonstop: the week became five days and each worker's day off was set by a colour or number. Spouses and relatives often rested on different days. In 1931 a six-day week followed, and the seven-day week with Sunday returned only in June 1940.

title.en: Forssmann threads a catheter into his own heart

lead.en: A young surgeon fed a tube into his own heart, then got an X-ray

summary.en: Forbidden to try the risky procedure, 25-year-old Werner Forssmann did it on himself: he pushed a catheter up a vein in his arm into his heart, then walked to the X-ray room to photograph it. He had to leave the clinic, and in 1956 received the Nobel Prize.

lead.en: Ploughed prairies turn to desert and farmers flee west

summary.en: Drought and the ploughing of prairies without soil protection turned the Great Plains into a desert; dust storms blotted out the sun and carried dust to the Atlantic. Hundreds of thousands of farmers fled west, as Steinbeck told in The Grapes of Wrath.

lead.en: Gandhi defies Britain's salt monopoly on foot

summary.en: In March and April 1930 Mahatma Gandhi and his followers walked about 390 km to the sea at Dandi to make salt in defiance of the British monopoly. The act of nonviolent civil disobedience drew worldwide attention to India's struggle for independence.

lead.en: Three great rivers overflow at once, drowning Wuhan for months

summary.en: In summer 1931 the Yangtze, Huai and Yellow rivers burst their banks, leaving Wuhan underwater for months. Drowning, famine and disease killed between 400,000 and several million people by various estimates. In September, Japan invaded Manchuria.

lead.en: Forced grain requisitions cause millions of deaths

summary.en: Collectivisation and forced grain requisitions caused mass famine in the Soviet grain regions. An estimated 5.7–8.7 million people died. In Ukraine the famine is known as the Holodomor, in Kazakhstan as the Asharshylyk.

lead.en: Thirty years of campaigns create a country named after a dynasty

summary.en: In 1902 Abdulaziz ibn Saud retook Riyadh with a small band of fighters, then conquered Najd, Ha'il and, in 1925, the Hejaz with Mecca and Medina. On 23 September 1932 his lands were united as the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia. Six years later commercial oil was found at Dammam, transforming the poor desert state beyond recognition.

lead.en: The army brings machine guns against emus, and the emus win

summary.en: In November 1932 Western Australian farmers asked the army to rid their fields of emus. Soldiers with two Lewis guns and 10,000 rounds fired 2,500 of them in six days, but the birds scattered in small groups. The commander compared emus to tanks, and the operation was dropped amid newspaper ridicule.

lead.en: The Nazis build a dictatorship within months

summary.en: On 30 January 1933 President Hindenburg appointed the Nazi leader Adolf Hitler Chancellor of Germany. Within months the Nazis banned other parties and set up a dictatorship that led to the Second World War and the Holocaust.

lead.en: The communist retreat that raised Mao to the top

summary.en: In October 1934 the Chinese communists' Red Army, encircled by Kuomintang forces, broke out of Jiangxi and fought its way some 10,000 km to Shaanxi in a year. Of roughly 86,000 who set out, only a few thousand arrived. During the march Mao Zedong rose to the top of the party leadership, and the march became a founding myth of the People's Republic.

lead.en: Mustard gas against spears, and a powerless League of Nations

summary.en: In October 1935 Mussolini, avenging the defeat at Adwa, sent his army into Ethiopia, which with Liberia was Africa's last independent state. The Italians used mustard gas on soldiers and civilians, and Addis Ababa fell in May 1936. Emperor Haile Selassie's speech to the League of Nations indicted Europe's inaction. Sanctions failed; the country was freed only in 1941.

lead.en: Mass arrests and executions sweep the Soviet Union

summary.en: In 1936–1938 the USSR conducted mass political repression, including the Moscow show trials. According to NKVD records, about 1.5 million people were arrested and some 680,000 executed in 1937–1938 alone.

lead.en: A rehearsal for WWII: the Republic against Franco

summary.en: In July 1936 General Franco led a revolt against the Spanish Republic. Germany and Italy backed the rebels, the USSR and the International Brigades the Republicans; Franco won in 1939 and ruled until 1975.

lead.en: The 'Tasmanian tiger' dies 59 days after gaining protection

summary.en: On 7 September 1936 the last known thylacine died at Hobart's zoo after being left outside its shelter on a cold night. The species had been granted protection just 59 days earlier. For decades farmers had killed the 'Tasmanian tiger' for bounties.

lead.en: An abstract model that underlies every computer

summary.en: In 1936 young mathematician Alan Turing described an abstract computing machine and proved that some problems cannot be solved by any algorithm. His universal machine became the theoretical foundation of every computer.

lead.en: A clash at Marco Polo Bridge becomes full-scale war

summary.en: A clash at the Marco Polo Bridge near Beijing in July 1937 escalated into full-scale war between Japan and China. Marked by atrocities such as the Nanjing Massacre, it killed millions and from 1941 merged into the Second World War.

lead.en: A response to a bombing becomes an anti-war icon

summary.en: Shocked by the German bombing of the Basque town of Guernica, Pablo Picasso painted a huge canvas in a few weeks for the Spanish pavilion at the 1937 Paris World's Fair. Guernica became an enduring symbol against war.

lead.en: Uranium splits — the road to nuclear power and the bomb

summary.en: In December 1938 Otto Hahn and Fritz Strassmann found that uranium nuclei split when bombarded with neutrons; Lise Meitner and Otto Frisch explained the process. The discovery led to both nuclear power and the atomic bomb.

lead.en: Britain and France hand Hitler the Sudetenland for "peace"

summary.en: In September 1938 Chamberlain and Daladier agreed to give Germany Czechoslovakia's Sudetenland without the Czechoslovaks at the table. Six months later Hitler occupied the whole country, and appeasement had failed.

title.en: The War of the Worlds broadcast

lead.en: Orson Welles 'reports the news' of a Martian invasion

summary.en: On 30 October 1938, the eve of Halloween, 23-year-old Orson Welles staged H. G. Wells's novel live on CBS as a string of breaking-news bulletins. The legend of nationwide panic is greatly exaggerated: newspapers inflated it, and historians still argue over how many listeners were really fooled.

lead.en: A trawler nets a fish known only from fossils

summary.en: In December 1938 a trawler captain showed museum curator Marjorie Courtenay-Latimer in East London a strange blue fish. Ichthyologist J. L. B. Smith recognised a coelacanth, a fish known to science only from fossils and thought long extinct. The species was named Latimeria after her.

lead.en: Germany invades Poland, starting history's largest war

summary.en: On 1 September 1939 Germany invaded Poland. The war between the Axis and the Allies engulfed much of the world and killed tens of millions, including the victims of the Holocaust. It ended with Germany's surrender in May and Japan's in September 1945.

lead.en: A secret protocol splits Eastern Europe into spheres of influence

summary.en: On 23 August 1939 the USSR and Germany signed a non-aggression pact with a secret protocol dividing Eastern Europe into spheres of influence. Germany invaded Poland on 1 September; Soviet troops entered its eastern regions on 17 September.

lead.en: A frozen-night tremor: Turkey's deadliest 20th-century disaster

summary.en: On the freezing night of 27 December 1939 a magnitude 7.8 quake on the North Anatolian Fault destroyed Erzincan, killing nearly 33,000 people, Turkey's deadliest natural disaster of the 20th century. In Europe, World War II was entering its fourth month.

lead.en: 872 days under siege, kept alive by the Road of Life

summary.en: From 8 September 1941 to 27 January 1944 German and Finnish forces besieged Leningrad for 872 days. Estimates of deaths from hunger, cold and shelling range from 600,000 to 1.5 million. Supplies came over Lake Ladoga by the 'Road of Life'.

lead.en: Nazi Germany murders six million European Jews

summary.en: In 1941–1945 Nazi Germany and its collaborators systematically murdered the Jews of Europe: in mass shootings in the occupied Soviet territories, in ghettos and in the death camps of Auschwitz, Treblinka and Sobibor. Around six million Jews were killed, along with hundreds of thousands of Roma, Soviet prisoners of war, disabled people and other victims of Nazi extermination policy.

lead.en: The Eastern Front opens as Germany strikes the USSR

summary.en: On 22 June 1941 Germany and its allies invaded the Soviet Union, beginning what Russians call the Great Patriotic War. The Brest Fortress garrison held out for weeks. The blitzkrieg was halted near Moscow in December 1941, and the Eastern Front became the main theatre of the war in Europe.

lead.en: Japan's strike pulls the US into World War II

summary.en: On 7 December 1941 Japanese aircraft launched a surprise attack on the main base of the US Pacific Fleet in Hawaii, killing about 2,400 Americans. The next day the United States declared war on Japan and entered the Second World War.

lead.en: A counteroffensive at the capital's gates drives the Germans back

summary.en: In October 1941 German forces launched Operation Typhoon against Moscow and came within about 30 km of the city. On 5 December the Red Army counter-attacked and by January 1942 had driven the enemy back 100–250 km.

lead.en: Paulus's army is encircled as the war turns

summary.en: From July 1942 to February 1943 the armies fought for Stalingrad on the Volga. The Soviet counteroffensive, Operation Uranus, encircled Paulus's Sixth Army, which surrendered on 2 February 1943. The battle was a decisive turning point of World War II.

lead.en: Minutes that turned the tide of the Pacific War

summary.en: American codebreakers had uncovered the Japanese plan to trap what was left of the US fleet at Midway Atoll. On 4 June 1942 dive bombers set three Japanese carriers ablaze within minutes, and a fourth was lost by evening. The US lost the carrier Yorktown. After Midway, Japan never regained the initiative in the Pacific.

lead.en: Montgomery halts Rommel and secures the Suez Canal

summary.en: In October and November 1942 Bernard Montgomery's British Eighth Army defeated Erwin Rommel's German-Italian forces in Egypt. The victory removed the threat to the Suez Canal and turned the tide of the war in North Africa.

lead.en: Six months in the jungle for a single airfield

summary.en: On 7 August 1942 US Marines landed on Guadalcanal and seized an unfinished Japanese airfield, later Henderson Field. For six months it was fought over on land, in the air and in night naval battles; the nearby strait was nicknamed "Ironbottom Sound" for its dozens of wrecks. In February 1943 Japan evacuated its remaining troops. It was the first major Allied offensive in the Pacific.

lead.en: After Prokhorovka the initiative passes to the Red Army for good

summary.en: On 5 July 1943 the Wehrmacht attacked the Kursk salient in Operation Citadel but was halted, with a major tank battle at Prokhorovka on 12 July. Afterwards the strategic initiative passed permanently to the Red Army.

lead.en: A dead 'Major Martin' with fake letters fools the Germans

summary.en: In 1943 the British dressed a dead vagrant as a fictitious Royal Marines officer, 'Major William Martin', and floated him ashore in Spain carrying 'secret' letters about landings in Greece. The Germans bought it and were caught off guard in Sicily. The idea traced back to a memo shaped by Ian Fleming, Bond's future creator.

lead.en: The largest seaborne invasion opens a second front

summary.en: On 6 June 1944 American, British, Canadian and other Allied troops landed on the Normandy coast in the largest seaborne invasion in history. The Second Front in Europe was opened, and the liberation of France soon followed.

title.en: Deportations of the peoples of the Caucasus and Crimea

lead.en: Whole peoples are branded traitors and exiled to Central Asia

summary.en: From November 1943 to the summer of 1944 the NKVD deported entire peoples, accused of collaborating with the Germans, within days each: the Karachays, Kalmyks, Chechens and Ingush, Balkars (8 March 1944), Crimean Tatars and Meskhetian Turks. They were shipped in freight cars to Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan and Uzbekistan, and tens of thousands died on the way and in the first years of exile. Their autonomies were abolished; most could return only in 1957, the Crimean Tatars only in the late 1980s.

lead.en: The end of the Tuvan People’s Republic

summary.en: The Uryankhay region on the upper Yenisei belonged to the Qing Empire until 1912 and then became a Russian protectorate. In 1921 the Tuvan People’s Republic was proclaimed there, formally independent but recognised only by the USSR and Mongolia. In 1944, at the request of its leadership, it joined the USSR as an autonomous oblast; today it is the Republic of Tyva within Russia.

lead.en: The Home Army battles the occupiers for 63 days

summary.en: On 1 August 1944 the Polish Home Army rose against the German occupation of Warsaw. After 63 days of fighting the insurgents surrendered; some 150,000–200,000 civilians died and the city was almost entirely destroyed.

title.en: Wojtek the bear at Monte Cassino

lead.en: A brown bear serves in the Polish army as a private

summary.en: Polish soldiers bought the cub Wojtek in Iran in 1942 and enlisted him as a private so he could board a ship. At Monte Cassino, his comrades recalled, he carried crates of shells, and he became the company’s emblem.

lead.en: Nuclear weapons are used in war for the first time

summary.en: On 6 August 1945 a US bomber dropped an atomic bomb on Hiroshima, and on 9 August another on Nagasaki. Well over 100,000 people died, many later from radiation sickness. Japan soon surrendered, and the world entered the nuclear age.

lead.en: Unconditional surrender ends the war in Europe

summary.en: After Soviet troops took Berlin, Germany's unconditional surrender was signed at Karlshorst late on 8 May 1945, already 9 May in Moscow. The date became Victory Day in the USSR, marking the end of the war against Germany.

lead.en: Nations create a body to prevent future wars

summary.en: On 26 June 1945 the Charter of the United Nations was signed at the San Francisco conference. The UN, formally founded on 24 October 1945, was meant to prevent future wars, with the USSR, US, UK, France and China as permanent Security Council members.

title.en: ENIAC, the first general-purpose electronic computer

lead.en: An 18,000-tube machine opens the computer age

summary.en: In late 1945 ENIAC came to life at the University of Pennsylvania — a 27-ton electronic computer with some 18,000 vacuum tubes. It calculated thousands of times faster than electromechanical machines and opened the computer age.

lead.en: A few lines read out on a porch in Jakarta

summary.en: On 17 August 1945, two days after Japan's surrender, Sukarno and Mohammad Hatta read a short declaration of independence outside Sukarno's house in Jakarta. The Netherlands tried to retake the colony, and four years of war and diplomacy followed. Only in December 1949 did the Dutch recognise the sovereignty of Indonesia, one of the largest nations on Earth.

lead.en: Stalin, Roosevelt and Churchill shape the post-war world

summary.en: On 4–11 February 1945, at the Livadia Palace near Yalta, the leaders of the USSR, the United States and Britain agreed on the defeat and occupation of Germany, Poland's borders, the creation of the UN and Soviet entry into the war against Japan. Yalta's decisions set the division of Europe into spheres of influence for the Cold War.

lead.en: An international tribunal tries the leading Nazi war criminals

summary.en: From November 1945 to October 1946 the International Military Tribunal set up by the USSR, the United States, Britain and France tried the leaders of Nazi Germany. Twelve defendants were sentenced to death. The trial first established crimes against peace and crimes against humanity and laid the foundations of international criminal law.

title.en: A melted candy bar and the microwave oven

lead.en: A candy bar melts by a radar set: the microwave oven is born

summary.en: Raytheon engineer Percy Spencer, who never finished grammar school, built magnetrons for radar. As the story goes, a candy bar in his pocket melted while he stood by a working set. Spencer began experimenting with food, and popcorn became the first food ever cooked by microwaves.

lead.en: The US and USSR rival worldwide without direct war

summary.en: After the Second World War the United States and the Soviet Union with their allies entered a global rivalry: the arms race, the Iron Curtain in Europe, wars in Korea and Vietnam, the space race. A direct war between the superpowers was avoided, and the rivalry ended with the Soviet collapse.

lead.en: British rule ends and Pakistan is born

summary.en: In August 1947 British India became independent and was partitioned into India and Pakistan. Partition brought the mass migration of millions and widespread communal violence. The end of the British Raj accelerated the collapse of colonial empires.

lead.en: A tiny semiconductor replaces the vacuum tube

summary.en: In December 1947 John Bardeen and Walter Brattain, in William Shockley's group at Bell Labs, built the first point-contact transistor. The tiny semiconductor device replaced vacuum tubes and made all modern electronics possible.

lead.en: The first space travellers were flies on a captured rocket

summary.en: Long before dogs, monkeys or humans, fruit flies went to space: scientists wanted to know how radiation affects living things. On 20 February 1947 flies rode a captured German V-2 rocket into space and became the first living things to come back alive.

title.en: Shepherds find the Dead Sea Scrolls

lead.en: A shepherd looks into a cave and finds the oldest Bible scrolls

summary.en: In the winter of 1946–1947 the Bedouin shepherd Muhammed edh-Dhib and his cousins found jars of scrolls about 2,000 years old in a cave by the Dead Sea, the oldest manuscripts of biblical books. Some of the scrolls were later sold through an advert in The Wall Street Journal.

lead.en: Six men cross the Pacific on a balsa raft in 101 days

summary.en: Thor Heyerdahl wanted to show that South Americans could have sailed to Polynesia. In April 1947 he and five companions left Peru on a balsa-log raft and covered 6,900 km in 101 days before smashing onto the reef of Raroia. All survived, and the film of the voyage won an Oscar.

lead.en: The UN sets out rights shared by all people

summary.en: On 10 December 1948 the UN General Assembly, meeting at the Palais de Chaillot, adopted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. For the first time it set out rights and freedoms common to all people, shaping international law ever since.

title.en: Founding of the State of Israel

lead.en: Ben-Gurion declares a state as war breaks out

summary.en: On 14 May 1948, as the British Mandate for Palestine ended, David Ben-Gurion proclaimed the State of Israel. Neighbouring Arab states went to war, and hundreds of thousands of Palestinian Arabs became refugees. The Arab-Israeli conflict became central to the region.

lead.en: American billions rebuild Western Europe

summary.en: In April 1948 the United States launched a European aid programme named after Secretary of State George Marshall. Over four years some 17 countries received about $13 billion to rebuild industry and trade. The USSR refused to take part and kept the Eastern European countries out, deepening the division of the continent.

lead.en: Israel's birth and the Palestinian exodus shape a long conflict

summary.en: The day after Israel declared independence on 14 May 1948, Egyptian, Transjordanian, Syrian, Iraqi and Lebanese forces entered Palestine. Israel prevailed and under the 1949 armistices held about 78% of the former Mandate; the West Bank went to Jordan and Gaza to Egypt. Some 700,000 Palestinian Arabs fled or were expelled — the Nakba, or 'catastrophe', for Palestinians; historians still debate its causes.

lead.en: An attack on one is an attack on all: the West unites

summary.en: On 4 April 1949 twelve North American and Western European states signed the North Atlantic Treaty in Washington. Its Article 5 on collective defence became the core of the Western bloc in the Cold War.

title.en: Founding of the People's Republic of China

lead.en: Mao proclaims a new state as the Kuomintang flees to Taiwan

summary.en: On 1 October 1949 Mao Zedong proclaimed the People's Republic of China from Tiananmen Square. The Communist victory in the civil war forced the Kuomintang government to retreat to Taiwan.

lead.en: The US nuclear monopoly ends and the arms race speeds up

summary.en: On 29 August 1949 the RDS-1 bomb was tested at the Semipalatinsk Test Site. The USSR became the second nuclear power after the United States, ending the US atomic monopoly and accelerating the arms race.
